I shipped a userland bridge for the two events that map cleanly today.

https://github.com/sjh9714/opencode-claude-code-hooks

Add the package directly to the OpenCode plugin array.

```json
{
  "plugin": ["opencode-claude-code-hooks"]
}
```

The bridge reads the existing Claude settings at runtime, maps OpenCode tool names to Claude matcher names, sends the Claude-shaped JSON payload on stdin, honors exit code 2 and structured deny results, applies `updatedInput`, and adds PostToolUse feedback to the tool result.

Users who want a dry run before installing the bridge can use the compatibility CLI in [dsh-movein](https://github.com/sjh9714/dsh-movein).

```sh
npx claude-to-opencode --hooks-only
npx claude-to-opencode --hooks-only --apply
```

I verified the bridge with real child processes and loaded the npm package through OpenCode 1.18.21. The published package is `opencode-claude-code-hooks 0.1.1`.

Known limits

- Stop is not bridged because `session.idle` has the timing problem already documented in this thread
- prompt, agent, HTTP, async, and conditional `if` handlers stay manual
- allow and ask decisions do not bypass OpenCode permissions
- this is a userland workaround, not a substitute for a native compatibility contract

Thanks for the review — all four points are fair and I've actioned them. Verified against the tree-sitter grammars directly:

**Point 1 (variable escape):** Confirmed, with one nuance worth flagging. `argPath`'s existing `dynamic()` guard (returns `true` for any `$`) means `> "$P"` bails to `undefined` → `!resolved` → the scan *skips*, so it does **not** prompt for a wrong path (fail-closed) — but the shell still executes the redirect because a redirection target isn't otherwise gated. So "mostly closed" is exactly right. A follow-up resolving shell vars before resolving would make it fully gated.

**Point 2 (PowerShell node name):** Confirmed — `tree-sitter-powershell` emits `redirection`/`file_redirection_operator`/`redirected_file_name`, not `file_redirect`. `descendantsOfType("file_redirect")` is a no-op there, so this scan is POSIX-shelves only. Noted in the comment now.

**Point 3 (misleading `tee` comment):** You're right — `tee` writes via command argument (FILES allowlist path), not `file_redirect`. Fixed the comment to describe what the scan actually covers (direct redirection targets) and note the remaining gaps (`dd of=`, `sponge`, `install`, `script -c`).

**Point 4 (spelling variance):** Confirmed via live parse: `>`, `>>`, `2>`, `2>>`, `&>`, `>&`, `<>` all parse as `file_redirect` with "last named child" correctly extracting the target (`&>`/`>&` have no `file_descriptor` child, so the positional read still works). `2>&1` degrades safely (`&1` doesn't resolve).

Pushed the comment fix as `ee7e83666`. Happy to add the per-spelling unit tests and extend to command-arg writes if you'd like this to be fully closed.

Still reproduces on **v1.18.21** (macOS arm64, headless `opencode run --format json`) — but the failure mode has changed since 1.18.19, and we can now answer the dropped-vs-clean question empirically. Setup: a local OpenAI-compatible fake provider; the **only** variable between runs is the shape of the SSE stream it serves.

**Three stream shapes, everything else held constant:**

| stream shape | behavior on v1.18.21 | terminal state |
|---|---|---|
| `finish_reason:"stop"` present (control) | 1 step, `step-finish reason:"stop"`, usage reported | exit 0, healthy |
| socket cut mid-body: 2 content chunks, connection aborted, no `[DONE]`, no finish chunk | SDK throws → retried with exponential backoff (gaps ≈ 2s → 4s → 9s → 19s, 5 attempts) | **visible `APIError` error event on the JSON stream, exit 1** — the v1.18.20 midstream-retry change works ✅ |
| clean drain: `[DONE]` sentinel sent, but **no non-null `finish_reason` anywhere** | **hot unbounded loop**: 982 turns in 38s (~26 turns/s), every `step-finish` is `reason:"unknown"` with all-zero tokens/cost, **zero error events, no backoff** | never exits on its own; had to be killed externally |

(A second run of the same clean-drain shape spun 1,661 turns / 88s before being killed.)

**To answer the two questions directly:**

1. **Yes, it still reproduces on ≥ v1.18.20 — but as a hang, not a silent success.** The midstream-retry change stopped the drained-empty stream from mapping to a completed turn *terminally*, but nothing catches it either: each turn still "completes" cleanly as far as the SDK can tell, so the prompt loop re-enters immediately — no cap, no backoff, no error. Against a real gateway, every spin re-sends and re-bills the full context window, so an overnight driver can burn significant spend per incident.

2. **The two cases are already distinguishable by behavior today.** A dropped/midstream stream throws inside the SDK and gets the proper retry-then-visible-error treatment (verified above — that path is fixed). A clean stream that ends without a finish reason throws *nothing*, so none of that machinery engages: it flows through as a finished turn carrying `finish: "unknown"`. The discriminator is right there in the payload: a clean drain whose finish is `"unknown"` with zero output tokens. Failing that shape as a retryable provider error would route the quiet case into the same backoff-and-halt path the dropped case already takes — which matches the approach in #43881.

Repro is a ~90-line Go server serving `chat.completion.chunk` frames in three modes against `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`; happy to attach the script plus the raw `run.jsonl` captures for all three runs if useful.

No blocking issues found.

Nit: packages/core/script/migration.ts:200-203 — `formatJson` hardcodes the prettier options (`parser: "json"`, `printWidth: 120`) rather than resolving the repo's shared prettier config. If the checked-in `.prettierrc` ever diverges (different print width, trailing-comma policy, etc.), regenerated snapshots will silently stop matching the prettier-styled copies again — the exact problem this fix addresses. Consider `prettier.resolveConfig` (or importing the shared config) so the two stay in sync automatically.

> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

- packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:52-66 — the decoder/encoder caches are keyed by schema object identity, which silently assumes a schema is never mutated after first execution — if a caller tweaks a schema after registration, the stale compiled decoder will validate against outdated rules. Worth adding a one-line comment documenting the immutability assumption, or freezing/asserting on first insert.
- packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:118-129 — `structuredClone` of the compiled JSON schema runs on every `inputJsonSchema`/`outputJsonSchema` call; for large schemas the clone can cost nearly as much as the `toJsonSchema` compile it replaces, especially where `definition()` is invoked per-request. Consider benchmarking, or returning the cached object directly and documenting that callers must not mutate (the added test currently guarantees freshness instead, which is the safer contract — just confirm both goals).
- packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:70-75 — the fallback output branch builds `Schema.decodeUnknownEffect(Schema.Json)` on every call while its siblings now cache; hoisting a module-level `const jsonDecode = Schema.decodeUnknownEffect(Schema.Json)` would keep the optimization consistent.
- packages/core/test/tool-schema.test.ts:174-198 — good freshness assertions; consider also a behavioral regression test that repeated executions through the cached decode/encode path produce identical success/error outcomes (e.g., the same invalid input rejected identically on the 1st vs 2nd call), protecting the WeakMap logic against future refactors.

> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

1. **packages/core/src/session.ts:616-619 (snapshot)** — A session row that has no event sequence yet makes `snapshot` die via `Effect.die(new Error("has no event sequence"))`. Why it matters: `die` is an unrecoverable defect, not an API error — imported/migrated sessions (or any path that inserts a SessionTable row without a corresponding event) would crash the request handler instead of returning a typed error.
